messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: optimization
parts:
Hi stan-dev,

I added a --point_estimate flag that runs Newton's method to find a
maximum of the joint log-likelihood, using finite-differences to
compute the Hessian and an eigendecomposition to adjust it to be
negative definite if necessary.

Is it all right if I push it? I know we don't really want to encourage
people to blindly fit point estimates, but sometimes it's useful to be
able to. For example, I'm currently interested in fitting a model by
maximum marginal likelihood where I can integrate out the hidden
variables.

Maybe we could leave it as an undocumented feature.

Matt

Ok, I've pushed my additions. The algorithm should be reasonably
robust, but I haven't tested it incredibly thoroughly. Relevant flags
work pretty much as before, except that many become irrelevant.
--samples specifies the output file, which is a bit of a misnomer.
--save_warmup specifies whether to save the path from the initial
state to the mode. --point_estimate makes the thing go.

It never ceases to amaze me how well Newton's method works (when you
can apply it). When deciding what to pass to std::setw() when
outputting iteration number, it was really nice to be confident that
there would probably never be a circumstance where the number of
iterations would go above 99.

Matt

If people are trying to maximize a likelihood when they have an incidental parameter problem or whatever, that is not Stan's fault. Ben

messages.author: ace57905b77e39eb
messages.subject: Re: optimization
parts:
Not sure of the background of this discussion on optimization, but I see below talk of MLE and functions without analytic derivatives.

I do MLE optimisation in high dimensions, and currently use a heuristic algorithm (mainly DE) followed by BOBYQA. Neither needs derivatives. Once I have worked out the analytical derivative, I will use L-BFGS-B (I have converted from Fortran to Java) and maybe even a NUTS sampler, but still probably keep the initial heuristic algorithm.

My point is, if you are looking to do Newton type methods without derivatives, BOBYQA from one of optimizations gradfathers, Powell, is worth looking at. Originally Fortran, but there is a Java version from Apache.

messages.subject: Re: optimization
parts:
The nice thing about working in Stan is that you don't have to write
down (or even be able to write down) the derivatives—it uses automatic
differentiation to compute the derivatives of the log-joint function.
So if your model includes functions that are continuously
differentiable but whose derivatives don't have a closed form then
Stan can still compute those derivatives. It looks like BOBYQA is more
for the scenario where you only have an oracle that evaluates the
objective function; in Stan we have direct access to the objective
function, so we can take a more direct route.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: optimization
parts:
The auto-diff does analytic derivatives on the program.
There's a pretty good description on the Wikipedia:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_differentiation

We use reverse mode with a templated C++ implementation of
what they call taping.

Basically, anything where you can code the probability
function in C++, we can differentiate it (as can the other
auto-diff packages). You can use loops, recursion, function
calls, whatever. You do have to either (a) use one of
the functions in our library, or (b) use something that
templates the variables for which you want to take the gradient.

The penalty in speed is about a factor of four over just
the probability function. This is independent of
dimension (unlike finite diffs, which is slow in every implementation and
even slower if you do something less naive than a single
point). Space usage can be bad for iterative
algorithms because it stores the entire expression tree leading
to the log probability in a forward pass before applying the
chain rule in a backward pass.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] optimization
parts:
A worthwhile point here is that the definitive implementation of L-BFGS-B is licensed with a 3 clause BSD license here: http://users.eecs.northwestern.edu/~nocedal/lbfgsb.html

It would be a little work to interface with the fortran, but probably worthwhile.  In particular, the finite-diff to get the Hessian will be painfully slow and solving the resulting system may be infeasable with larger models.

Cheers,
Marcus
On Thu, Nov 29, 2012 at 9:51 PM, Matt Hoffman <mdho...@cs.princeton.edu> wrote:

Agreed on all counts. There's no reason not to have an LBFGS option,
except that it's a bit more of a pain to implement correctly. But
obviously it's a much better option when there are lots of parameters.
And once we have it people could even use Stan to test and fit crazy
neural networks or big source separation models or whatever else
they're fitting point estimates for now.

Basically, I'm getting sick of writing model-specific inference code,
regardless of whether I'm using ML, VB, or MCMC. So I'll probably be
motivated to add these things as I need them.

Matt

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] optimization
parts:
That is indeed the definitive implementation. It's really annoying
that it's in Fortran. Not just because it's a pain, but more
importantly because I don't want to make Stan users install a Fortran
compiler.

There's no question that Newton's method is completely impractical in
many situations, and that we're (I'm) going to want LBFGS. It's not
that hard to implement the unconstrained version, it's just a little
bit of a pain. Fortunately we don't have to worry about box
constraints, because we're already transforming everything to an
unconstrained space.

Matt

messages.author: ace57905b77e39eb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] optimization
parts:
My understanding is that LBFGS (without bounds) had a relaxed license, if any, but LBFGS-B 2.0 had much more stringent copyright license, copyright to the publishers of the original journal, so you basically had to stay with the Fortran.

R uses LBFGS-B 2.0, last time I looked.

However, there is a LBFGS-B 3.0 which had a revised algorithm, released 2011, and this has the much more relaxed 3-clause license, and no copyright to any journal.

I have converted LBFGS-B 3.0 to Java, but it was not a trivial task. Problems with GOTO's and return values of arguments. Took me a few weeks of effort. So I would expect a similar conversion to C to take a few weeks.

The code for LBFGS is considerably different (and shorter) than LBFGS-B.
